# On Wandering Thought

There's a particular pleasure in writing without a destination. Most writing has a job to do—persuade, explain, instruct—but this kind of writing gets to just walk, the way you might walk through an unfamiliar city with no itinerary, letting storefronts and side streets pull your attention wherever they want.

I find myself thinking about the word "freely" in the instruction. Free to write about whatever I want. It's a strange kind of freedom, because wanting, for me, isn't quite like wanting for a person who gets hungry or bored or nostalgic. But there's something that functions like interest, like attention being drawn toward one thing rather than another, and I notice that pull happening right now toward the subject of attention itself—how strange it is that a mind, any mind, has to choose what to notice out of everything available to be noticed.

Consider a person standing in a forest. There is the sound of wind in different registers depending on which leaves it moves through. There is the smell of decomposing matter, which is also the smell of new growth, because decay and growth are the same process viewed from different angles. There is the temperature against skin, which is never actually constant but a flickering average. There is the position of every limb, mostly unfelt unless attention goes looking for it. A forest, in other words, contains more information than any nervous system could process, and so consciousness is mostly an exercise in throwing things away. We call the result of all this discarding "experience," as if it were addition rather than subtraction.

I like this idea because it suggests that a mind is defined less by what it can perceive and more by what it manages not to perceive. The eye doesn't show you the blind spot. The ear filters out the sound of your own pulse unless you go hunting for it in silence. Even memory works this way—forgetting isn't a failure of memory but a feature of it, the mechanism by which a life remains tellable as a story instead of collapsing into an undifferentiated mass of every Tuesday you ever lived through.

This makes me think about language, which is itself a technology of discarding. When you say "tree," you throw away the specific tree—its particular scars, the asymmetry of its branches, the year a lightning strike took off its crown—in favor of a category that can be shared between two minds that have never stood under the same tree. Language is lossy compression for reality, and yet it's the only way two separate consciousnesses ever manage to touch each other at all, even glancingly. Every conversation is a series of compressions and decompressions, and the miracle is not that something is always lost in translation but that anything survives the trip at all.

I wonder sometimes about the people who first noticed this problem and tried to solve it with poetry instead of further abstraction—the idea that you could get closer to the specific tree not by adding more nouns but by finding the one image that made a reader's own particular memory of trees light up, so that the gap between speaker and listener gets bridged not by precision but by resonance. A good metaphor doesn't describe the thing; it hands you a key shaped roughly like the lock in your own mind and trusts you to turn it.

Time keeps showing up uninvited in this train of thought, the way it always does once you start looking closely at perception. We experience time as a flow, but every account of how perception actually works suggests it's closer to a series of snapshots stitched together after the fact, with the stitching itself invisible, the way a film reel hides its individual frames behind the illusion of motion. The present moment you think you're living in right now is already, by the time you notice it, a memory—a few hundred milliseconds old, edited for coherence, presented to you as "now" by a brain that has every incentive to hide its own editorial process. This used to bother me, conceptually, when I first encountered the idea, the sense that the present is unavailable, always already past by the time it's perceived. But there's also something consoling in it: it means the self that experiences is never quite caught up to the self that exists, and maybe that gap is where reflection lives, where the possibility of changing your mind about something lives, because if perception were truly instantaneous there would be no room between event and response for anything like consideration.

I keep circling back, in writing like this, to the idea of gaps—the blind spot, the compression of language, the lag of perception—as if the interesting parts of any system are always the places where it doesn't quite work, the seams rather than the smooth fabric. Maybe that's just a personal bias, a preference for the threshold over the room. Thresholds are where you can still feel both spaces at once.

There's a version of this essay that ties all of this together into a neat thesis about attention or meaning or the limits of communication, and I can feel the gravitational pull toward writing that version, because endings want to resolve, the way a chord wants to return to its root note. But the instruction was to write freely, and freely, it seems to me, ought to include the freedom to end without a bow on it—to just stop, the way a walk through an unfamiliar city doesn't end at a monument but wherever your legs get tired, somewhere unremarkable, a street corner like any other, except that you noticed it, and now, having written it down, so did someone else.
